beliefs.practice: Read the connection string only from a runtime secret store or environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never hard-code, commit, or log the URI/credentials.
Always connect using TLS/SSL and verify the server certificate; configure the MongoDB driver to require TLS and reject unauthorized certificates in production.
Use connection pooling with a tuned maxPoolSize and socketTimeoutMS matching your concurrency needs; avoid creating one client per request — reuse a shared client/process-wide pool.
Implement exponential backoff with jitter and honor server-provided Retry-After headers for transient failures and 429 rate-limited responses rather than aggressive immediate retries.

Store embeddings as float32 arrays in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding) and avoid indexing them as text; create a vector index specifically for that field (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) with parameters tuned to embedding dimensionality and recall/latency tradeoffs.
Normalize embeddings consistently (e.g., L2-normalize) if you intend to use cosine similarity so index distance metric and scoring match how embeddings are compared at query time.

When ingesting long product documents, chunk them into 200–500 token segments, compute embeddings per chunk, and store chunk metadata (product_id, chunk_id, token_count, source) to enable retrieval, reranking, and prompt construction.
Create secondary (non-vector) indexes on frequently filtered metadata fields (e.g., product_id, locale, language, created_at) to make pre-filtering before vector search efficient.
Use bulk/ordered=False bulk inserts for initial ingestion to speed up loading large sets of chunks and catch/record per-item failures rather than stopping the whole batch.
Limit returned document fields using projection to only the fields needed for the prompt (text, product_id, metadata) to reduce network transfer and serialization cost during retrieval.

During vector search retrieval, fetch the top-N (e.g., 5) candidate chunks by vector score and then run a small text-based reranker or heuristic filter using metadata and token budgets before constructing the LLM prompt.

Keep prompts under the LLM token limit by summing token_count fields of candidate chunks and trimming lowest-score chunks until the context fits; store and use token_count per chunk to do this cheaply.

Choose a partition key that evenly distributes writes and reads (e.g., hashed product_id or product_category depending on access patterns) and avoid high-cardinality hot keys; test performance with realistic traffic.

Keep the embedding vector field out of text indexes and do not create both a full-text index and a vector index on the same field; vector indexes should be declared via the cluster’s vector indexing APIs/settings.

Instrument and monitor query latencies, index build times, memory and disk usage, and rate-limited (429) occurrences; use explain() and the MCP/documentdb tools to validate that queries are using the intended vector/index.

Use optimistic concurrency / versioning (e.g., etag or version field) or MongoDB update operators to avoid races when updating documents (do upserts with an idempotency key for repeated ingestion runs).
Keep sensitive PII out of embeddings and stored chunk text when possible; if PII must be stored, use field-level encryption or server-side encryption with customer-managed keys.

Tune vector index parameters (e.g., M and efConstruction for HNSW or nlist for IVF) according to embedding dimension and target recall/latency, and validate with a representative recall/latency benchmark set.

Use explain plans and indexStats to confirm that vector/metadata filters are applied and to detect full-collection scans; after creating indexes, re-run ingestion or compacting steps if required by the cluster to make indexes active.

Version embeddings, schema, and indexes (store embedding model name + version in chunk metadata) so that when you upgrade the embedding model or change chunking you can reindex or filter old vectors safely.
